preamble: Clues are of two types. In the acrosses, the definition part leads to the answer to be entered and the (cryptic) remainder leads to an anagram or reversal of the answer, usually of one word. In the downs, the cryptic part leads to the answer to be entered and the definition part leads to an anagram or reversal of that answer, also usually of one word.

clue.text: Falconer's frame caught a pike

parts.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
taken as written
a ged is the Scots name for the pike, the fish

explanation.surface: A falconer's carrying frame snares a pike, as if hawking gear doubled as fishing tackle.
explanation.walkthrough: Across entries come from the definition; the wordplay spells CAGED, which this puzzle's rule rearranges into the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: In falconry a cadge is the portable wooden perch on which several hooded hawks are carried to the field.

clue.text: State of applied science to study disadvantage in modified rye

definitions.note: defines TECHNOCRACY, the anagram of the entry

parts.note: to con is to study or learn by heart

indicators.note: in sets the drawback word inside the rearranged grain
modified means the letters of rye are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
a catch is a hidden snag or disadvantage

explanation.surface: A technocratic state studies the drawbacks of genetically modified rye.
explanation.walkthrough: In the downs the wordplay gives the entry and the definition leads to its anagram, TECHNOCRACY. A cony-catcher was an Elizabethan swindler.
explanation.definitionFit: A technocracy is a state governed by technical experts, the practitioners of applied science.

clue.text: Slav maybe, cold in a rocky height

definitions.note: defines CROAT, the anagram of the entry

indicators.note: in places the cold letter inside the phrase that follows

parts.note: taken as written
a tor is a rocky hill or crag, especially on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A Slav, perhaps, shivering on top of a rocky summit.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives the entry; the definition leads to CROAT, its anagram, as the down rule says.
explanation.definitionFit: A Croat is a native of Croatia, one of the South Slavic peoples, so a Slav by way of example.

clue.text: Perished climbing last bit of Parnassus with lateral faces

definitions.note: defines SIDED, the anagram of the entry

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing means the word is written upwards, so reversed

parts.note: died means perished

indicators.note: last bit of picks the final letter of the mountain's name

parts.note: taken as written: the letter comes from Parnassus

explanation.surface: Climbers perished near the summit of Parnassus, on its steep flanks.
explanation.walkthrough: Down entries need not be words: DIED written upwards plus the S gives the entry, and the definition leads to SIDED, its anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A solid that is sided has flat sides or lateral faces, as in a six-sided figure.

clue.text: Salad harvest holds me up

definitions.note: defines MELANGE, the anagram of the entry

indicators.note: holds means the gathering word wraps round the next piece

parts.note: to glean is to gather or harvest leftover grain

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read upwards, so reversed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A salad crop is holding me up.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives the entry, an old word for a minstrel; the definition leads to MELANGE, its anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A melange is a mixture or medley, so a salad in its figurative sense of a jumble.

clue.text: Consults together about independence due to lord's superior

indicators.note: about sets the consulting word around the single letter, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: to confer is to consult together
I is short for independence, as in the UDI of a breakaway colony

explanation.surface: Vassals confer about breaking free from what they owe their overlord's overlord.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay spells CONIFERS, which the across rule rearranges. Forinsec is a term from feudal law.
explanation.definitionFit: In feudal law forinsec service was owed to the superior lord rather than the immediate one, so it was due to a lord's superior.

clue.text: Measure of elastance one's enveloped in white paint

definitions.note: defines DARAF, the anagram of the entry: the unit of elastance, farad spelt backwards

indicators.note: enveloped in means the single letter is wrapped inside the paint word

parts.note: fard is white paint for the face, an old cosmetic
one's is one is, and one is a, the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A measure of elasticity: someone is wrapped up in a coat of white paint.
explanation.walkthrough: Down entries need not be words: the wordplay gives the entry, and the definition leads to DARAF, its anagram, the reciprocal of the farad.
explanation.definitionFit: The daraf is the unit of elastance, the reciprocal of capacitance, named by spelling the farad backwards.

clue.text: Gold box to be worthy of rich chocolate cake

definitions.note: defines SACHERTORTE, the anagram of the entry

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry
a chest is a large box
to rate is to deserve or merit, as in 'rates a mention'

explanation.surface: A gold box fit to hold a rich chocolate cake.
explanation.walkthrough: In the downs the wordplay gives the entry and the definition leads to its anagram, here SACHERTORTE.
explanation.definitionFit: Sachertorte is the rich Viennese chocolate cake layered with apricot jam, first made at the Hotel Sacher.

clue.text: By reason of this, being old-fashioned, the lady's getting up to dine

definitions.text: By reason of this, being old-fashioned
definitions.note: defines HEREAT, the anagram of the entry; being old-fashioned marks the word as archaic

indicators.note: in a down clue getting up means the word is read upwards, so reversed

parts.note: her means belonging to the lady
to eat is to dine

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned excuse: the lady is getting up to have her dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives the entry; the definition leads to HEREAT, its anagram, as the down rule says.
explanation.definitionFit: Hereat is an archaic adverb meaning at this, or because of this.

clue.text: Snooze before afternoon betel

definitions.note: defines PAAN, the anagram of the entry

indicators.note: before puts the snooze ahead of the afternoon's letter

parts.note: a nap is a short snooze

explanation.surface: A doze before an afternoon chew of betel.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives the entry, a soft leather; the definition leads to PAAN, its anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Paan is betel leaf wrapped round areca nut and spices, chewed after meals in India.

clue.text: Childless? Grieve no more — it's lovely!

parts.note: s.p., for sine prole, is the genealogist's mark for dying without issue
rue is to grieve or regret; no more flags that sense as old-fashioned

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives the entry, the channel through which molten metal runs into a mould; the definition leads to SUPER, its anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Super! is an exclamation of delight, as when something is declared lovely.

clue.text: Spy, a hundred, having repose with maturity (11, two words)

definitions.note: defines SECRET AGENT, the anagram of the entry

parts.note: cent comes from the Latin for a hundred, as in per cent
rest is repose
age can mean maturity, as in 'come of age'

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives the entry; the definition leads to SECRET AGENT, its anagram, as the down rule says.
explanation.definitionFit: A secret agent is a spy working undercover, usually for a government.

clue.text: Shift completely round, describing spots of colour

parts.note: a core is a miner's shift or spell of work, a Cornish mining word

parts.note: all means completely, as in all alone

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds CORELLA, an Australian cockatoo, which the across rule rearranges into the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Ocellar means relating to ocelli, the eye-like spots of colour on a peacock's tail or a butterfly's wing.

clue.text: Pass snake, going round sheltered side

indicators.note: the snake goes round the sheltered side, so its letters enclose that word

parts.note: the asp is the Egyptian cobra
lee is the side sheltered from the wind

explanation.surface: Advice to let a snake slither past by slipping round to the side out of the wind.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds ASLEEP, which the across rule rearranges into the entry. 'Pass' looks like a mountain pass but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Time is said to pass or go by; the entry is the verb for time slipping away.

clue.text: Drags up something with hawk on the end?

definitions.text: something with hawk on the end?
definitions.note: defines LEASH, the anagram of the entry: a falconer's hawk is tethered by one

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is written upwards, so reversed

parts.note: to hale is to drag or haul, as in haled into court

clue.text: Row, touching, about sex appeal

indicators.note: about wraps the word for touching around the next piece

parts.note: re, as in a letter heading, means concerning or touching on
it is old slang for sex appeal, as in the It girl

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay makes RITE, rearranged into the entry by the across rule. 'Row' tempts as a quarrel; it is a line.
explanation.definitionFit: A tier is a row or rank, as in the tiers of seats in a theatre.

clue.text: Old surgeon, always painful

parts.note: Ch abbreviates chirurgeon, the old word for a surgeon, as in ChB, the surgery degree
ay is an old word for always, as in for ay

explanation.surface: A surgeon of the old school who is forever in pain.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds CHAY, a chaise, which the across rule rearranges into the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Achy means aching, sore all over, as a body feels with flu.

clue.text: Distinctive phrase sung, part of melody learnt

indicators.note: part of shows the letters lie inside the run of clue words that follows

parts.note: the letters run across the end of melody and the start of learnt

explanation.surface: A singer masters a distinctive phrase, part of a tune learnt by heart.
explanation.walkthrough: The hidden word is ODYLE, an old name for a supposed natural force, which the across rule rearranges into the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A yodel is a song or call with distinctive leaps between chest voice and falsetto, sung by Alpine herders.

clue.text: Mostly bombastic American falls in Canada

parts.note: tall talk is boastful, bombastic talk
US abbreviates the United States, so American

explanation.surface: An overblown American describes some Canadian waterfalls.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay makes TALUS, a slope of rock debris, rearranged by the across rule. Sault is Canadian French for a waterfall, as in Sault Ste Marie.
explanation.definitionFit: In Canada a sault is a waterfall or rapid, from the old French word for a leap.

clue.text: Support energy plan

parts.note: aid is help or support

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds AIDE, an assistant, which the across rule rearranges into the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: An idea can be a plan or intention, as in 'the idea is to leave early'.

clue.text: Watery bundle beside river

indicators.note: beside puts the river's letter right next to the bundle

parts.note: a bale is a large bound bundle, of hay or cotton

explanation.surface: A soggy bundle of hay left lying by the river.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay makes BALER, a machine that bales hay, rearranged by the across rule.
explanation.definitionFit: Blear describes eyes that are dim and watery, as in blear-eyed.

clue.text: We have brushes, look, and we'll be around rising master

definitions.note: defines LOWRIES, the anagram of the entry: a lowrie is a fox in Scots, and a fox's tail is its brush

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look

indicators.note: be around means the first word wraps round the reversed title

parts.note: we'll is we will, so the clue's own we supplies the outer letters

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means the word is read upwards, so reversed

parts.note: sir is a title of respect, what a pupil calls the master

explanation.surface: Foxes speak: look, we'll gather round the master as he gets up.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives the entry; the definition leads to LOWRIES, its anagram. Lowrie, from Tod Lowrie, is a Scots name for the fox.
explanation.definitionFit: Lowries are foxes in Scots, and a fox's bushy tail is called its brush.

clue.text: Classical verse Chalcis adapted about love, more fitting (13, two words)

indicators.note: about means going round, so the rearranged town name wraps the letter for love
adapted means altered into a new form, so the letters of the town's name are rearranged

parts.note: love is nil in tennis scoring, written as the letter O
more fitting means apter, the comparative of apt

explanation.surface: A scholar reworks a poem about the Greek town of Chalcis, finding love the most fitting theme.
explanation.walkthrough: In this puzzle the across wordplay yields a jumble of the entry, not the entry itself: a rearrangement of CHALCIS (here CHALICS) placed about O, then APTER, gives thirteen letters the across rule rearranges into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alcaic strophe is a four-line stanza form named after the Greek poet Alcaeus and used by Horace, so it is classical verse.

clue.text: Radioactive element in meadow touching vital organs

definitions.note: defines RENAL, the anagram of the entry

indicators.note: in places the element's symbol inside the meadow word

parts.note: a lea is a meadow or grassland
Rn is the chemical symbol for radon, a radioactive gas

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives the entry, which need not be a word; the definition leads to RENAL, its anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Renal means concerning the kidneys, among the body's vital organs.

clue.text: Stick together mostly when tackling special tasks (tedious)

mostly means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: to cohere is to stick together

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives the entry, meaning to pamper; the definition leads to CHORES, its anagram.

clue.text: Odd bits of nitre in erbium alloy

indicators.note: in sets the picked letters inside the chemical symbol

parts.note: taken as written: the letters are picked from nitre

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay makes ENTER, which the across rule rearranges into the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Terne is an alloy of lead with a little tin, used to coat sheet steel as terneplate.

clue.text: Trunks, rarely part of chariot superstructure

indicators.note: part of shows the letters lie inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of chariot and the start of superstructure

clue.text: Listener's a townie, old

definitions.note: a listener is an ear, so listener's means of the ear

parts.note: a cit is an old contemptuous word for a townsman, short for citizen

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay makes CITO, Latin for quickly, rearranged by the across rule. 'Listener's' looks possessive but works as an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Otic means relating to the ear, the organ a listener hears with.

clue.text: Singers stop when in credit after one

definitions.note: defines CHOIR, the anagram of the entry

indicators.note: after means what follows comes after the numeral for one
in sets the stop word inside the credit abbreviation

parts.note: ho is a call to stop, as in whoa

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives the entry, the fluid said to run in the veins of the gods; the definition leads to CHOIR, its anagram.

clue.text: A liquor incorporating recipe with embellishment at table

definitions.note: defines GARNI, the anagram of the entry: garnished, of a dish

indicators.note: incorporating means the spirit takes the recipe letter into itself

explanation.definitionFit: Garni describes a dish served garnished, as in steak garni, so it comes with embellishment at table.

clue.text: Sun coming up — because of being inside here's product of combing

definitions.note: defines NOILS, the anagram of the entry

indicators.note: inside means the short piece goes within the reversed sun
in a down clue coming up means the word is read upwards, so reversed

parts.note: Sol is the sun, from the Latin
in can mean because of being, as in 'in failing he learned'

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives the entry; the definition leads to NOILS, its anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Noils are the short fibres removed when wool or silk is combed, a by-product of combing.

clue.text: Extremely distressful moment succeeded fine

explanation.definitionFit: Crise is the French word for crisis, a turning point of acute distress, used in English in phrases like crise de nerfs.

clue.text: Eyes fixed, taking in chapter

parts.note: set means fixed, as in a set date

explanation.definitionFit: Tecs are detectives, slang shortened from detective, and private detectives are called private eyes.

clue.text: Slang, American, seen in 'dreck'?

explanation.definitionFit: Argot is the jargon or slang of a particular group, such as thieves' cant.

clue.text: King historically holds height

parts.note: has means holds or possesses

explanation.definitionFit: Shah was the title of the hereditary monarch of Iran until the revolution of 1979.

clue.text: Like Paddy, endlessly chewed leaf

explanation.definitionFit: Siri is betel, the peppery leaf wrapped round areca nut and chewed as a stimulant across South Asia.

clue.text: Old Scottish chopper: one turned in the chopping

indicators.note: in places the reversed piece inside the rearranged short word
chopping means the letters of the short word are cut up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: turned means the word for one is reversed

parts.note: an ace is a one on dice or playing cards

explanation.surface: An old Scots axe: one spun round in the middle of the chopping.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds HECATE, the Greek goddess of witchcraft, which the across rule rearranges into the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: An eatche is an adze, the old Scots name for the axe-like tool used to dress timber.

clue.text: Thoroughly garbled sign, worrying

parts.note: out means completely or thoroughly, as in tired out

indicators.note: garbled means the letters of sign are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Garbled signage is thoroughly unsettling.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay makes OUTSING, to sing better than, rearranged by the across rule. To touse is to pull about, as a dog worries a rat.
explanation.definitionFit: Tousing means hauling about or worrying, the way a terrier shakes and tousles its prey.

clue.text: Soak got up round end of bender — he mends well?

parts.note: to ret flax is to soak it to loosen the fibres

indicators.note: round puts the rising word around the final letter of bender

parts.note: rose means got up

indicators.note: end of picks the last letter of the word that follows

parts.note: taken as written: the letter comes from bender

explanation.surface: A drunk got up after a bender: is he someone who repairs things nicely?
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay makes RETRORSE, meaning turned backwards, rearranged by the across rule. The question mark flags a definition by description.

clue.text: Having imbibed third of litre, judged tight

indicators.note: having imbibed means swallowing, so a letter goes inside the word for judged

parts.note: seen means judged or regarded, as in 'seen as unfair'

indicators.note: third of picks the third letter of the word that follows

parts.note: taken as written: the letter comes from litre

explanation.surface: Having downed part of a litre, someone was judged to be drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay makes STEEN, to line with stone, rearranged by the across rule. 'Tight' suggests drink but means taut.
